title: Indian-Origin NASA Astronaut Sunita Williams Harvests Fresh Vegetables on the Space Station
excerpt: Williams shares a video of her space farming efforts aboard the ISS, where she has been cultivating lettuce as part of NASA's research into sustainable food production for long-duration missions.
body:
• Indian-origin NASA astronaut Sunita Williams has harvested fresh vegetables aboard the International Space Station and shared a video of her efforts, describing it as "cooking on the space station."
  • The vegetable cultivation is part of NASA's Plant Habitat research program, which studies how crops grow in microgravity to develop sustainable food systems for future deep-space missions.
  • Williams, whose father was born in Gujarat before emigrating to the United States, has spoken about the cultural importance of food and mealtimes during her time in orbit.
  • The research builds on decades of ISS plant experiments and complements Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla's 2025 SPROUTS study, which grew moong and fenugreek in space.

Indian-origin NASA astronaut Sunita Williams has harvested fresh vegetables aboard the International Space Station and shared a video showing her efforts at what she described as "cooking on the space station," according to a report by NDTV. The moment captured both a scientific milestone and a personal one for one of the most accomplished astronauts of Indian heritage.

Growing Food 400 Kilometers Above Earth

Williams has been cultivating crops aboard the ISS as part of NASA's ongoing plant growth research program. The experiments use the station's Veggie and Advanced Plant Habitat systems — compact, LED-lit growth chambers that allow astronauts to plant, tend, and harvest leafy greens in microgravity conditions.

https://x.com/NASA/status/2089367348608225574

Previous harvests on the ISS have included "Outredgeous" red romaine lettuce, Chinese cabbage, mizuna mustard, and dwarf tomatoes. The research examines how water availability, light cycles, and the absence of gravity affect plant development, nutritional content, and food safety.

NASA considers space farming essential for future long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where resupply from Earth would be impractical. Fresh produce supplements freeze-dried rations while providing psychological benefits to crew members spending months in isolation.

"Food in the Indian culture is super important. Mealtime is the time, of course, when everybody gathers, but it means so much to have somebody prepare food for somebody else and give it to them as a gift."

— Sunita Williams, NASA astronaut

A Career Spanning Decades in Space

Williams, born in Euclid, Ohio, to an Indian-Gujarati father and a Slovenian-American mother, has been a fixture in American space exploration for over two decades. She holds the record for the most spacewalks by a female astronaut and has logged hundreds of days in orbit across multiple missions.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ul_N5SE4A3w

Her connection to Indian culture has been a recurring theme throughout her career. She has previously spoken about finding Indian dishes on the standard ISS menu and how the flavors reminded her of growing up at home with her family. In a NASA video celebrating Asian American and Native Hawaiian Pacific Islander Heritage Month, Williams gave a tour of the ISS kitchen and discussed the cultural significance of sharing meals in space.

Building on India's Space Farming Legacy

Williams's vegetable harvest comes roughly a year after Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla conducted the Sprouting Salad Seeds in Space (SPROUTS) experiment during the Axiom-4 mission in June and July 2025. Shukla sprouted green gram and fenugreek seeds — staples of the Indian subcontinent — in microgravity, analyzing their growth patterns, nutritional quality, and microbial content.

NASA described the SPROUTS study as "an important first step toward accommodating the unique dietary needs of Indian crew members" and noted its potential to inform advances in controlled environment agriculture on Earth.

Together, Williams's ongoing vegetable cultivation and Shukla's seed-sprouting experiments represent a growing body of research that could eventually allow astronauts to grow culturally diverse crops in space, supporting crew nutrition and well-being on missions lasting months or years.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For the Indian diaspora, Williams remains one of the most visible symbols of Indian-American achievement in science and exploration. Her space farming work bridges two themes close to the community: the cultural centrality of food and the pride in India's expanding role in space research, from ISRO's interplanetary missions to Gaganyaan, the country's planned crewed spaceflight program.
